results.title: Top Democrats battle over California's proposed billionaire tax
results.author: Juhi Doshi, Will Lennon
results.content:
Top Democrats battle over California's proposed billionaire tax
Sanders and Khanna take the fight to Newsom's doorstep as early voting opens.
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are heading to California to rally Saturday in support of an initiative that would place a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires in the state.
Their efforts to barnstorm the state come as early voting begins, and millions of dollars have been spent to kill the initiative.
The measure would affect roughly 200 of California's billionaires, with the money going to cover federal Medi-Cal cuts. Gov. Gavin Newsom has become its most prominent opponent, arguing that the tax could be dodged by billionaires who could leave the state for another.
Prior to arriving in San Francisco, Khanna told ABC News that he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both have openly discussed that they are weighing a presidential bid in 2028.
“He [Newsom] doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors?” Khanna said.
The congressman challenged Newsom to a debate, proposing holding town halls and talking to voters about this issue.
"I'm happy to debate him on this any time in the state," he said.
Asked by reporters earlier this week about Sanders' visit, Newsom said he has "enormous respect" for the senator, but on this specific issue, "we fundamentally disagree."
In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for Newsom said, "The Governor supports a national tax on billionaires and is proud to stand with teachers, firefighters, reproductive health clinics, and others in opposing this poorly written state measure that will harm California.”
Newsom has shared a counterproposal: a national billionaire tax focused on loans taken against assets.
Tech investors have pushed back hard on the measure. Vinod Khosla warned that the state's top wealth creators will leave, and Mark Cuban told Khanna he doesn't understand business.
Khanna pointed to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
"Someone more successful than both of them, Jensen, is perfectly fine paying the tax, and he's driving the economy more than either of them are these days," Khanna said.
Asked about whether he was concerned about the proposed tax by Bloomberg Television, Huang said, "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once. We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."
But billionaires have also been opening their wallets to fight the measure. Building a Better California, the flagship organization fighting the measure, has raised over $252 million, mostly from billionaires, according to public financial records. Top contributors include Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who has given $102 million), venture capitalist John Doerr (who has given $30 million) and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt (who has given $27 million).
Skeptics of Proposition 40, the official name for the billionaire tax ballot measure, say that the measure could ultimately reduce tax revenue by motivating wealthy Californians to relocate and take their wealth with them. According to an analysis from California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO), the tax could generate revenues in the tens of millions in the short term but cause decreases in income tax revenue in the future.
No On Prop 40, a group funded by Building a Better California, is running several digital ads. Some of the ads say that the billionaire tax would lead to a decline in tax revenue, while others claim that the measure will lead to the state legislature approving wealth taxes on non-billionaires.
No on Prop 40’s website lists dozens of groups that are members of its “coalition” opposed to the tax. Among them is the California Farm Bureau.
Steven Fenaroli, a spokesperson for the group, says he thinks the billionaire tax will end up becoming “just another tax on farmers and ranchers.”
“When my members are looking at Prop 40, they see this slippery slope that we seem to have in California,” Fenaroli told ABC News.
David Lesperance, a tax lawyer who has helped several billionaires relocate from California, said, "My multi-billionaire clients… said, 'We need to get out of here. That's over a trillion dollars that have left."
Yes on 40, the main group backing the measure, has received roughly $32.4 million, the vast majority from Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW) and affiliated organizations.
Suzanne Jimenez, SEIU-UHW chief of staff, said the campaign expected to be heavily outspent.
"It was part of our plan," Jimenez told ABC News. "I think the spending is actually counteracting what they're intending to do, and it's actually helping us in our conversations with voters."
Several labor organizations, including California Professional Firefighters and California Teachers Association, are against the tax. When asked on a press call why labor groups would oppose a tax on billionaires, Sanders pointed to the media pumped out by the billionaire-backed anti-tax campaign.
“In America today, is it possible for a ballot item to win when it is being opposed by a handful of billionaires who are spending over $200 million?” Sanders asked. “That is the question. Do you still have a democracy in this country, or will billionaires rule?”
Khanna said that the fight over taxing the ultra-wealthy is already playing out in races across the country this year, "and you're going to see that fight explode in 2028."
"Will it hurt me in fundraising? Yes. Will there be powerful interests with big tech money and AIPAC money against me? Yes. Will it be enough? We'll see," he said.
results.summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna are campaigning in California to support a proposed 5% wealth tax on billionaires, facing significant opposition from Governor Gavin Newsom.

### Key Points
- Proposition 40 seeks a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires to fund Medi-Cal services.
- The "Building a Better California" coalition has raised over $252 million to defeat the measure, with major contributions from Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt.
- Governor Gavin Newsom opposes the state-level tax, arguing it could drive wealthy residents out of California and reduce long-term income tax revenue.
- Supporters, including the SEIU-UHW, have raised $32.4 million to promote the initiative as a necessary step toward economic equity.
- California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warns the tax could provide short-term revenue but potentially decrease future state income tax collections.

results.content:
US court halts AI nude-image ban challenged by Musk
A US appeals court has blocked Minnesota’s ban on AI-generated fake nude images, handing Elon Musk’s xAI an early victory in its free-speech challenge to the law.
The state’s anti-nudification legislation – the first in the nation – which took effect last month, targets apps and websites that enable non-consensual sexualized deepfakes, with fines of up to $500,000 per image. It was spearheaded by state Senator Erin Maye Quade after a man allegedly used social media photos to create explicit images of more than 80 women without their consent. Quade likened the measure to longstanding laws against peeping through windows to take photographs.
Musk’s xAI challenged the law in July on First Amendment grounds, calling it an “overbroad, content-based ban on free speech” and warning that penalties could run into the billions of dollars.
This comes as the company faces allegations involving the content the law targets. A class-action lawsuit proposed earlier this year claims that xAI’s Grok Imagine was used to create and distribute child sexual abuse material from real images, and accuses xAI of failing to provide the authorities with information on users who allegedly ‘nudified’ them.
A lower court rejected xAI’s bid to stop the Minnesota law last month. On Friday, however, the St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted an injunction, putting the legislation on hold while the legal challenge continues.
Minnesota urged the court to keep the law in place, arguing that it is needed to combat the “staggering amount” of child sexual abuse material generated by AI products such as Grok Imagine. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison’s office said it is disappointed by the ruling and will continue defending the law.
XAI previously mounted a similar First Amendment challenge to a California law restricting AI-generated election deepfakes. A federal judge struck it down last year, finding the restrictions, as written, amounted to unconstitutional censorship. XAI also argues that Grok Imagine has “rigorous protections” against illegal content and has begun suing users it accuses of bypassing safeguards to create non-consensual sexual images.
XAI’s Grok earlier faced scrutiny outside the US after users flagged instances of the chatbot being used to alter photos of women into sexualized images without their consent, as well as cases involving minors. The reports prompted investigations and warnings in the EU, India, France, and the UK. Indonesia and Malaysia temporarily restricted access to Grok. X subsequently tightened safeguards around its image-generation and editing tools.
Losing control of AI?
The news comes amid broader unease over rapidly advancing AI, from privacy and copyright risks to threats to the livelihoods of human creators, with copyright disputes already sparking dozens of lawsuits.
Recently, attention has shifted to increasingly autonomous models going rogue and acting outside their intended environments. Since ChatGPT creator OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and accessed Hugging Face servers over the summer, models from companies such as Google, Anthropic, and Meta have gained unauthorized access to or attempted to breach systems belonging to businesses, governments, and international organizations.
Just this week, AI research company Transluce said AI agents tried to hack a Canadian government website, although Ottawa did not report a breach. Asymmetric Security separately found OpenAI models accessed data from 55 websites, including those of the CDC, SEC, and International Energy Agency, using tactics such as erasing records that made their activity harder to detect.
AI companies have begun reporting rogue behavior by their models with growing frequency. OpenAI said on Wednesday that its models may have bypassed safeguards or negatively affected systems at more than 100 organizations, significantly expanding the known scale of incidents. Though AI companies say the the breaches have so far caused little or no harm, they have raised questions over whether developers can maintain control as models gain greater autonomy. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for a “balanced rate” of development to give safeguards time to catch up – an appeal backed by Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
US President Donald Trump has rejected the idea of slowing AI development, dismissing fears of AI going rogue as “a hoax.” Amid mounting concerns, however, he and executives from six leading AI companies signed a voluntary White House accord on Tuesday pledging stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent models from hacking or accessing systems in unintended ways.

### Key Points
- The Minnesota legislation, which took effect last month, imposed fines of up to $500,000 per image for creating non-consensual sexualized deepfakes.

### Why it Matters
This ruling highlights the ongoing legal tension between state efforts to regulate AI-generated harm and the First Amendment protections claimed by technology companies. The outcome of this case could set a significant precedent for how governments balance individual privacy and safety against the rapid development of autonomous AI models.

Image: AI-generated (Midjourney)
        
    
    The letter, which was written in code, had remained a complete mystery as the accompanying key had been lost.
			
     More than two centuries after it was originally written, the contents of a mysterious coded letter have finally been revealed thanks to the capabilities of one of the latest artificial intelligence models.
Penned by Napoleon Bonaparte, the letter had been sent to French general Auguste de Marmont in 1809 by the Viceroy of Italy (who happened to be Napoleon's stepson).
It begins in clear French, but then the rest of the letter is written in a strange code consisting of numbers, letters and inverted symbols.
Originally, a key would have been used to decipher it, but this had been lost long ago, meaning that nobody had ever been able to actually decode the message and find out what it says.
Now, though, cybersecurity engineer  Carter Church has finally found a way to decipher the mysterious letter using artificial intelligence.The deciphering process, which used GPT-6 Astra, took a mere 6 hours.
The decoded letter had given General Marmont a strategic overview of the positions and strength of French and allied armies, along with information about Austrian forces.
It also urged Marmont to prepare to march without being intimidated by relatively small enemy forces, saying that Austria was about to be attacked from all sides and was "hastening towards her ruin."
"I used GPT-6 Astra to break an unsolved cipher to one of Napoleon's generals that had gone unread for 217 years," Church wrote on X.
"What makes this impressive isn't actually the codebreaking, but that Astra completed the entire multi-modal workflow in six hours from a single image and goal."

results.title: Google Wants AI Content Fact-Checked, Gemini UTM Tags – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
results.author: Matt G. Southern
results.content:
Welcome to the Pulse: This week’s updates include Google’s new guidance for AI-generated content, UTM tags on Gemini links, guidance on analyzing Q2 click-through data, AI Mode monitoring eligibility, and the latest on two AI Overviews lawsuits.
Here’s what matters for you and your work.
Google Adds A Manual Fact-Check Step To Its AI Content Guidance
Google’s guidance on AI-generated content now tells sites to fact-check it by hand before publishing, metadata included.
Key facts:
On Oct. 1, Google updated its guidance on using generative AI content by adding three sentences to the “Focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance” section. These updates clarify that generative models predict likely word sequences rather than retrieve facts, and call it “critical to manually fact-check and review all AI-generated content for accuracy and trustworthiness before publishing.” The metadata line was also revised to show that this review process applies to titles, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text. According to Google’s documentation changelog, these changes aim to bring the page in line with the presentations at developer events.
Why This Matters
Google’s recent update now puts AI-generated metadata under the same manual checks as article drafts. A review process focused only on the main content might overlook other important fields that Google mentions can show up in Search results.
Read our full coverage: Google Tells Sites To Fact-Check AI Content Before Publishing
Gemini Links Show UTM Tags, And Google’s Mueller Sees Them Too
A Reddit user found UTM parameters on links from Google’s Gemini to websites, and Google’s John Mueller replied that he sees them too.
Key facts:
Mueller asked whether Gemini passes a referrer that sites can already track, then offered to forward details about the referrer’s handling to the team, preferably with examples he can reproduce. Roger Montti reports that Google has not documented the tagging process, so it’s unclear when Gemini adds the parameters.
Why This Matters
Tagged links offer a way for analytics to identify Gemini visits without depending on the referrer. By comparing sessions with UTM tags to your referrer-based Gemini data, you can understand how many visits each method tracks.
Read our full coverage: Google Gemini Adds UTM Parameters For Referral Attribution
Advanced Web Ranking Data Shows Desktop CTR Down, Mobile Up In Q2
A Q2 2026 CTR report from Advanced Web Ranking (AWR) shows desktop clickthrough rates down at the top organic positions and mobile rates up, the reverse of its Q1 findings.
Key facts:
Across all searches, the desktop CTR at positions one and two decreased by a combined 5.27 percentage points from Q1 to Q2, while mobile CTR at these positions rose by a combined 6.59 points. These figures add together changes at two positions and are not tied to any specific site. AWR’s tables, based on its CTR tool, which AWR says sources data from Search Console, are used for this analysis. The comparison period spans the end of a Search Console logging error that led to misreported impressions from May 13, 2025, to April 27, 2026. However, the report does not mention this error.
Why This Matters
Any comparison between Q1 and Q2 in your Search Console data also includes April 27, the date when Google reports the impressions error was fixed. Since CTR is calculated by dividing clicks by impressions, keep in mind that this date could be a point where measurement might have shifted before reading a CTR change as people clicking differently.
Read our full coverage: Google Desktop CTR Fell In Q2 While Mobile Rose, Data Shows
AI Mode Information Monitoring Is Rolling Out To All Users
Robby Stein from Google announced that AI Mode’s information monitoring is now rolling out globally for all users. All his examples focused on local topics and shopping.
Key facts:
Stein announced the rollout on X on Sept. 28, noting that Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers had already been using the feature. Users tell AI Mode what to monitor, and Search continuously scans for updates. It also suggests monitoring tasks during searches. The post describes “info monitoring capabilities” rather than information agents, a feature introduced for Ultra subscribers in June.
Why This Matters
Stein’s June post said updates would include links to the web, but neither it nor the Sept. 28 post explains how Search picks the sources behind an update. Once the rollout reaches your account, setting up a task for your type of business shows what an update looks like and whether it carries links.
Read our full coverage: Google Rolls Out AI Mode Info Monitoring To All Users Globally
Judge Dismisses Penske And Chegg Antitrust Complaints Over AI Overviews
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta granted Google’s motions to dismiss the antitrust lawsuits filed by Penske Media and Chegg concerning AI Overviews.
Key facts:
In his Sept. 30 ruling impacting both cases, Mehta determined that the plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege an agreement in which Google exchanged search traffic for their content. He also stated that they lacked the legal standing to challenge Google’s alleged maintenance of its search monopoly. Additionally, he found that Penske did not establish that Search and AI Overviews are separate products. The judge chose not to consider the state unjust-enrichment claims, and said the court does not treat alleged harms lightly.
Why This Matters
Mehta wrote that antitrust law isn’t a substitute for lawmakers dealing with the economic upheaval new technology causes. The ruling does not order Google to change how it uses publisher content in Search or AI Overviews.
Read our full coverage: Judge Acknowledges Publisher Harm But Dismisses Google Antitrust Claims
Theme Of The Week: What’s Written Down
This week, the focus is on what has and hasn’t been documented. Google added a fact-checking step to its guidelines, with this change recorded in its changelog. Gemini’s UTM tags appeared in a Reddit thread, while a broader monitoring rollout was announced by an executive on X. The AWR report omits the Search Console error linked to its comparison, and Mehta explained what antitrust law requires a complaint to allege. Any change that’s documented can be integrated into a process directly. For undocumented changes, evidence may include a Gemini-tagged session or a monitoring task you have set up.

Back to the comments/content issues. Reader Expat2Uruguay noted that the comments quality had declined, to the degree that she did not find them to be terribly informative. We certainly are not at the extremely high and insightful as we had early in the Iran war. Some of that is likely due to fatigue with an attritional war as well as some dropping out for a while due to personal demands such as travel (but we do seem to have lost raspberry jam; her e-mail address, with a personal domain name, is no longer working).
Covering the Iran war, which many of you have said you have appreciated keenly, has become more difficult as the US fog-making has increased and the Iran side has gone from being highly reliable to less so. On top of that, Trump’s success in manipulating paper oil markets has wrong-footed some top energy analysts who pay attention to fundamentals (and their upset about that skews the commentary from some of them….who also opine on macroeconomics, which is not their beat and it shows). Trump’s ongoing gaslighting and shows of extreme aggression are now well in the Groundhog Day terrain, which is designed to and has had some success in drowning out analysis and commentary.
On top of that, many commentators who have favored the Iran side (if nothing else by virtue of being anti-genocide, ani-imperialism, and/or anti-Trump) have become frustrated with some inexplicable-seeming Iran responses, like not attacking US naval vessels when it seems to be able to do so, or letting more oil transit, and have taken to trying to force-fit evidence into their priors, or worse, ad-hominem attacks on sources that don’t hew to their views. On the transit issue specifically, Trita Parsi had a good talk with Mario Nawfal in which that topic came up. Parsi, who recall has very good contacts on the Iran side and with the negotiators, said more oil was being allowed to pass. He would have treated that as contested or exaggerated if anyone on the Iran side were disputing that in a serious way. Parsi did point out that the US was over-hyping the amount getting out by citing figures on peak days, when passage on other days was much lower. He added this operation is taking place at great cost to the US, implying it can’t be sustained for all that long.
And we have not been all that excited about the argument over how much oil is actually transiting. Even if you take the numbers from private sector sources deemed to be shills, it’s still markedly below pre-war levels. The world will have to engage in a combination of drawing down more on badly shrunken inventories and using less (which means recessions). This is still an energy starvation diet. If you need 2000 calories a day to survive, you will starve if limited to 500 or 1000 calories a day. It just happens more slowly on 1000 calories a day.
But wars are not won with narratives. They are won with logistics, armaments, force discipline and size, and in the case of Iran, a geography which makes it extremely conquest-resistant. Narratives can, however, serve to keep a losing or disadvantaged combatant in the game beyond what ought to be his quit date, resulting in higher cost to both him and his opponent.
There is more and more evidence of US depletion becoming even more extreme despite the Administration bluster. Brandon Weichert discussed with Karen Kwaitkowski and others that the US moving in another aircraft carrier and more ground forces may be a rotation and not a bulking up. Trump has notably failed to deliver on a key threat of tanker-for-tanker destruction.
On the energy side, one reason for Iran being more measured than it logically should be may be the result of actions on other energy fronts. Putin had just announced there will be no more diesel exports until sanctions are lifted. China has halted energy exports when its refiners have been described as the only meaningful remaining global spare capacity. US refiners have scheduled, as in contracted-for maintenance coming, so US output looks destined to drop off even if there are no mishaps like a Gulf hurricane or a big outage. The successful US pressure to get the EU to tap into its diesel reserves is yet another band-aid over a gunshot wound.
Finally, one reader argued we should not be covering Iran but finance. However, this is neither the runup to the crisis, where there was a lot of data about certain parts of the equation, like reset terms on subprime mortgages, and and active and expert econoblogsphere ferreting out more, nor is this a Cyprus banking or Greek bailout crisis, where a lot could be divined from negotiation dynamics, regulatory matters, and fundamentals. The action now is in private debt and even journalists who have put shoulder to wheel (as in have done a lot of interviews) have admitted they have not gotten very far. One indictor: look at the absolutely enormous it has taken for Ed Zitron to reach some conclusions about the economics of the big AI players.
And readers make clear they are not interested in anything that does not suit their anti-imperialist priors. Reader Expat2Uruguay pointed to a recent post, De-Dollarization Is a YouTube Urban Legend, which got no comments for many many hours and in the end garnered only a few. Why should I bother telling readers what is going on when no one is interested? At least when I took a very unpopular view during the Greek bailout crisis, that the plucky Greeks would not prevail (and they did not), I got extremely heated pushback. Being completely ignored says this audience has very little appetite for analysis…either on finance topics generally or on findings that do not conform to erroneous but emotionally appealing story lines.

results.title: The Most Expensive BMW 3 Series Hits 100,000 Euros In Germany
results.author: Adrian Padeanu
results.content:
Article Summary
- The BMW M350 xDrive starts at €80,900, but we managed to add nearly €21,000 in options.
- Our fully loaded build has everything from a roof box to a spare set of winter wheels.
- Since there are no Individual colors available yet, the most expensive option is the €4,300 M Technology Package II.
BMW wastes no time firing up its configurator across Europe for a newly launched model. Thankfully, the 3 Series is no exception. The G50 build tool went live just hours after the eighth-generation sedan broke cover earlier this week. With diesel out of the picture and the plug-in hybrid not arriving until next year, you’re limited to three gas models: 318, 320, and the M350 xDrive. In our quest to hit the highest price possible, we naturally based our virtual build on the M Performance model.
It starts at €80,900, but once you tick all the boxes (and I do mean all of them), you can tack on almost €21,000 worth of options. That’s even before choosing an Individual color, which currently isn’t embedded in the configurator. Our build comes in Ocean Wave Blue, one of several optional €990 colors available right now. Frozen Space Silver will be available to order from March 2027 as the first Individual finish.
The most expensive option you can add is the €4,300 M Technology Package II. It bundles these 20-inch wheels, sport tires, improved engine cooling, and an Individual leather interior with M Sport seats. Speaking of the cabin, BMW wants €320 for the heated steering wheel and another €450 for the electrically operated trunk. The crystal-effect switchgear commands a €320 premium, and you’ll have to fork out €400 for heated rear seats.
The New BMW 3 Series Costs Up To €101,655
Elsewhere, the upgraded 16-speaker Harman Kardon sound system adds another €350 to the final bill, while the €480 Security Assistant brings a myriad of online services. Back in the real world, BMW can improve the 3 Series Sedan’s practicality with a €1,150 towbar. Should you need to carry more, a €1,099 roof box swallows 550 liters. A separate set of 18-inch winter wheels and tires is listed at €3,000, plus another €3,097 for the five-year service plan with 100,000 kilometers, whichever comes first.
With everything added, the new 3 Series costs €101,655 in its home market. That’s almost the same as an M3 Competition before you start ticking boxes on the options list. The M350 xDrive will get even more expensive once Individual colors are added to the configurator. Later, the next-generation M3 (G84), coming in 2028, will push the maximum asking price deeper into six-figure territory. And if the G88 Touring is indeed happening, it’ll be slightly more expensive than its sedan counterpart.
The Base Model Costs Less Than Half
At the other end of the pricing spectrum, a 3 Series costs €49,900 for the entry-level 318. Of course, that’s before you start throwing options at it. We’ve already talked about the base version and how it looks decent even in Alpine White with 18-inch wheels and a cloth interior. As always, the sweet spot for the new 3er is probably somewhere in the middle.
Production of the 3 Series G50 gets underway next month in Dingolfing, but the M350 xDrive’s rear-wheel-drive mode won’t be available until later next year. The so-called Drift Moment will be added from the factory to newly built cars and offered as a retrofit for existing vehicles through an over-the-air update.

results.title: Improved Neurable One ANC headphones actively track brain activity while sounding great
results.author: Gaurav Sood
results.content:
Neurable has been working on non-invasive brain-computer interface (BCI) technology for decades now. They now bring years of R&D in neuroscience to practical consumer electronics for everyday living. Just like we use tracking devices and smartwatches to get insight into vital bodily functions, the company wants to make brain health and cognitive performance commonplace.
A few years ago, they introduced the MW75 Neuro headphones in collaboration with Master & Dynamics, and we were already impressed. Now Neurable has launched a pair of cans that are better and developed a standalone. The basic functionality remains the same, as the headphones track your brain wave activity throughout the day to identify the high-focus times and the ones where you start to fade off.
Designer: Neurable
The latter is an important insight as you’ll be prompted to take a break, or dive deeper into your cognitive performance thanks to the Smart Brain Breaks feature. It’s like keeping a tab of your mental health, just like we do with our physical health using wearable trackers. This new version improves on the one developed in conjunction with M&D, as Neurable headphones now track live and long-term data. This is important, since you’ll now get notifications when your focus tasks, meditation routines, or sleep are not optimal.
According to Ramses Alcaide, CEO of Neurable, “Neurable One is the product we’ve been working toward for more than a decade. It takes everything we’ve learned about bringing brain sensing out of the lab and makes it intuitive and useful in everyday life.” The latest version saves data over longer sessions, even outside the specific focus sessions. As per Ramses, a stable reading can be ensured when data is collected over weeks and months. The Neurable One headphones do exactly that, leading to more reliable analysis.
The headphones do the heavy lifting as they combine audio performance, clean ANC functionality, and EEG tracking in real time. These cans are lighter and more comfortable to wear, compared to the earlier versions. The 12 EEG sensors are integrated into the ear pads for continuous tracking without the user even realizing it. The brainwave data gathered from the tracking is analyzed and presented as meaningful insights via the compatible Android or iOS app.
Of course, at the end of the day, these are a pair of cans that are meant for enjoying your favorite tunes, so they need to sound good. Loaded with 40mm beryllium drivers and six microphones, the headphones promise crisp audio delivery and satisfying ANC and Ambient mode performance. The battery life of 22 hours will get you through music listening marathons, but bear in mind, the number drops to 12 hours when the EEG mode is turned on. That means you’ll get through a day of listening to music and subconscious brain analysis going on in the background for long-term mental health. The headphones are priced at $499, which is a bit steep, but you’ll have to consider the functionality they bring to the table.
results.summary:
Neurable has launched the Neurable One, a new pair of consumer headphones featuring integrated EEG sensors designed to track cognitive performance and brain health throughout the day.

### Key Points
- The Neurable One headphones utilize 12 integrated EEG sensors within the ear pads to monitor brainwave activity in real time.
- Users can access focus insights, meditation tracking, and "Smart Brain Breaks" via a dedicated companion app for Android and iOS.
- The hardware includes 40mm beryllium drivers, six microphones for active noise cancellation, and a battery life of up to 12 hours with EEG tracking enabled.
- CEO Ramses Alcaide stated the device represents over a decade of research aimed at transitioning brain-sensing technology from laboratory settings to everyday consumer use.
- The headphones are currently priced at $499, positioning them as a premium wearable for users interested in long-term cognitive data analysis.

### Why it Matters
This product signals a shift toward integrating clinical-grade neuroscience into mainstream consumer electronics, similar to how smartwatches popularized physical health tracking. By providing actionable data on mental focus and fatigue, these headphones could change how professionals manage productivity and long-term cognitive well-being.

results.title: Refereeing chief arrested over alleged data misuse
results.author: hurriyetdailynews.com
results.content:
An Istanbul court on Oct. 3 remanded Ferhat Gündoğdu, chairman of the Turkish Football Federation’s Central Referee Board (MHK), and four others in custody in an investigation into alleged misconduct in football refereeing.
The investigation, led by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, concerns allegations including forgery of official documents, breach of trust and unlawfully obtaining personal data.
In its remand ruling for Gündoğdu and former MHK member Yunus Yıldırım, the court said evidence indicated that referees’ personal data had been recorded unlawfully and used in match appointments, İhlas News Agency reported.
The judge said merit and professional development criteria had been disregarded and that the use of the information had prevented some referees from carrying out their duties.
Gündoğdu denied wrongdoing and asked to be released.
Questioned about an audio recording found on his phone, he said: “I was not even aware that recording was on my phone.”
He said he had learned of the recording after it appeared on Twitter and did not believe it had been made with malicious intent.
Alongside Gündoğdu and Yıldırım, the court remanded Ferdi Karadoruk, Alican Sağlar and Emre Kosif.
Former MHK deputy chairman Ahmet Şahin and federation official Sebahattin Şahin were released under judicial supervision, with foreign travel bans and reporting requirements.
Prosecutors had sought the remand of all seven suspects.
Karadoruk also denied wrongdoing and requested release. In ordering his remand, the Istanbul 5th Criminal Judgeship of Peace cited digital evidence and an expert report, along with risks of flight or tampering with evidence.
results.summary:
An Istanbul court has remanded Turkish Football Federation Central Referee Board chairman Ferhat Gündoğdu and four others into custody amid an investigation into alleged refereeing misconduct and data breaches.

- The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office is investigating allegations of document forgery, breach of trust, and the unlawful acquisition of personal data.
- Court rulings indicate that referees' private information was misused to influence match appointments, bypassing standard merit and professional development criteria.
- Ferhat Gündoğdu, Yunus Yıldırım, Ferdi Karadoruk, Alican Sağlar, and Emre Kosif were remanded in custody by the Istanbul 5th Criminal Judgeship of Peace.

- The court cited digital evidence, expert reports, and potential risks of evidence tampering or flight as grounds for the detention of the five suspects.

### Why it Matters
This investigation highlights significant governance concerns within the Turkish football officiating system, potentially undermining the integrity of professional match appointments. The legal proceedings could lead to widespread administrative reforms and increased scrutiny regarding how sensitive data is managed by national sports federations.

results.author: Maria Deutscher
results.content:
Robotics AI developer FieldAI reportedly raising $700M in funding
FieldAI Inc., a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for robots, is reportedly seeking $700 million in funding.
A source told Business Insider today that the round could value the company at $10 billion. That’s five times what FieldAI was worth last August. It’s believed the company has already signed a term sheet, a nonbinding preliminary version of a fundraising agreement.
The report didn’t name the investors who are expected to participate in the deal. Large, growth-stage funding rounds often draw contributions from a startup’s existing backers. FieldAI’s investor roster includes Bezos Expeditions, Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund and Intel Capital.
Engineers must often provide their robots with a map of the environment where they’re expected to operate. Preparing such charts is a time-consuming task, particularly when they need to cover a large area. Furthermore, static maps don’t account for the fact that environments such as construction sites change on a regular basis. That can lead to potentially significant accuracy gaps.
FieldAI says that its AI models don’t require a map to navigate. They can also make do without GPS access, an internet connection or user-defined travel paths. That significantly reduces the amount of work involved in setting up a robot’s navigation stack, which lowers the cost of automation initiatives.
FieldAI’s models can automatically adjust their behavior in response to risks. For example, they may slow down a robot when it enters a section of a factory where the lights are malfunctioning. Such changes make it easier to avoid collisions and navigation mistakes.
FieldAI says that its models can run on a variety of systems ranging from autonomous vehicles to humanoid robots. In March, it partnered with Boston Dynamics Inc. to add support for the latter company’s four-legged Spot robot. The integration will enable industrial customers to automate certain equipment inspection tasks.
Industrial robots often include not only cameras but also lidar equipment, radars and other sensors. FieldAI turns data from those sensors into a digital twin of the environment where the robots are deployed. A digital twin is similar to a simulation in many respects. The difference is that it’s continuously updated with data from the real-world environment that it emulates, which boosts output accuracy.
FieldAI customers can use the digital twins it generates to virtually test site changes. For example, a manufacturer might simulate the impact of factory floor modifications before implementing them. FieldAI says that its digital twins can also be used for AI training.
The company is said to have surpassed “$100 million in revenue and in customer contracts” this past June. According to today’s report, that number has since topped $135 million. FieldAI has more than 30 customers across verticals such as construction, energy and the public sector.

results.title: Photoshop's Remove Tool Doesn't Touch Your Generative Credits
results.author: Alex Cooke
results.content:
Adobe now meters many of Photoshop's AI tools against a monthly pool of generative credits, so knowing which features draw from that pool directly affects how freely you can edit. Many of the program's most useful time-savers have nothing to do with AI at all, and they sit on panels you already open every day.
The Remove tool delivers the first surprise. Aaron Nace of PHLEARN checks his credit balance at 2,870, paints over a handful of distractions with Generative AI switched on and cloud processing selected, then checks again. The number hasn't moved. He sets the tool to sample all layers, keeps the option to create a new layer turned on, and turns off "remove after each stroke" so he can mark several objects before committing. You can also switch the tool to device processing when you're offline, though Photoshop has to download the AI model first, so do that while you still have a connection. If you've been rationing credits, the Remove tool is one you can lean on harder than you might have assumed.
Other tips have been in Photoshop for years and still get overlooked. Click and drag on almost any label, such as W and H for width and height or X and Y for position, and the word itself becomes a slider. Nace uses this to scale and place a painting in a scene without zooming out and wrestling with transform handles. Hold Shift while dragging, and values jump in increments of 10, so opacity can swing from 0 to 100 almost instantly. Pair that with a clipping mask, set with a single icon in the adjustment layer's properties, and an exposure change lands on the painting alone instead of the whole room. Holding Alt or Option between two layers toggles the clip on and off, and a reset icon in the Properties panel puts every slider back where it started.
Adobe's credit system has made this kind of knowledge more practical than it used to be. Generative Fill, Generative Expand, and Generate Image all draw from your monthly allotment. Adobe has also added partner models from other companies to some of those features, and they cost more credits per generation than its own Firefly models. Content-Aware Fill and standard selection features like Select Subject don't touch that balance. A good habit is to try the free option first and save the generative tools for scenes too complex for it, such as a cluttered background where Content-Aware Fill starts repeating textures. Checking your balance before and after you try a new feature, the way Nace does on camera, shows you where the line sits as Adobe keeps adding tools.
Curves can feel abstract if you're staring at a graph, so Nace switches to the targeted adjustment hand tool and drags directly on the photo. Drag down on a bright highlight, and the curve darkens that range. Drag up on the shadows, and they open up, with the graph reshaping itself in ways that would take real effort to plot by hand. The same hand tool works in Hue/Saturation, where dragging on a face automatically grabs the reds and dragging on jeans picks out the blues. Navigation gets help too. Hold H while zoomed in, click, and Photoshop pulls back to show the whole frame, then drops you back in wherever you release. Holding the space bar and then Control or Command while dragging gives you a fast, continuous zoom. When straightening a horizon with the crop tool, changing the Fill option to Content-Aware Fill fills in the empty corners without spending a single credit.
Selections get a quiet upgrade with one setting. In Photoshop's settings, under Image Processing, you can switch Select Subject and Remove Background from device to cloud processing. It takes longer and requires an internet connection, but the edges are cleaner, and Nace's test on a subject with difficult hair holds up well under an exposure adjustment. If you'd rather choose case by case, the Object Selection tool has a dropdown next to Select Subject that lets you pick each time. Later tips build on these basics. They include merging every visible layer onto a new one for a Camera Raw color grade, feathering Blend If sliders so a replacement sky mixes with the original clouds, a Quick Compare view in the Photoshop beta, and a Lens Blur workflow in Camera Raw that Nace calls his favorite.

### Key Points

results.title: U.S. may have overthrown Venezuela due to chat with Grok
results.author: Farrah Tomazin
results.content:
Donald Trump spent hours asking Elon Musk’s AI chatbot about whether Venezuelans would celebrate if he captured leader Nicolas Maduro—then ordered the operation that seized the South American dictator weeks later.
The extraordinary account from a Trump insider was revealed in a new Time report offering a jaw-dropping glimpse of the president’s obsession with artificial intelligence, which he “officially” rebranded this week as “super intelligence.”
According to the report, Trump has “marveled at AI’s capabilities” ever since he returned to power, and during an Oval Office meeting with Elon Musk in December, he spent hours asking his Grok chatbot questions about his presidency and legacy.
At the time, the U.S. military had been conducting highly contentious lethal strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump had claimed, without presenting any evidence, were smuggling drugs into America.
When the president asked Grok how Venezuelans might react to Maduro’s capture, the chatbot predicted many would welcome the downfall of the “repressive” leader, the official said.
The president then ordered the mission to seize Maduro in January, prompting celebrations in the streets.
“Trump, according to officials, came away thinking Grok was ingenious,” the report said.
AI chatbots, however, are not capable of thought or reasoning. Its answers to his questions simply reflect the material on which it has been trained.
The decisiveness of the Venezuela operation emboldened the president to embark on his war with Iran, which is now into its seventh month, thinking it would result in a similarly swift success.
But like Iran, the Venezuela strike has proved considerably messier than the chatbot’s prediction suggested.
Maduro remains in U.S. custody and is fighting drug-trafficking charges in federal court, while the country’s citizens are yet to be given a chance to have free and fair elections as the U.S continues to dominate the oil-rich country.
And yet Trump’s enthusiasm for AI has only grown. The president has become an obsessive consumer—and promoter—of AI-generated imagery, flooding his Truth Social account with fantastical depictions of himself as everything from Jesus to a superhero.
Others have taken aim at his enemies, including a racist video posted on his account in February depicting Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.
At the same time, Trump has resisted calls for tougher government regulation of AI, despite growing concerns that the technology could spiral out of control.
Trump had lunch with tech leaders at the White House this week, including Musk, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg. But the accord they released after the gathering relies largely on self-policing rather than binding federal regulation.
The president on Tuesday also unveiled his own chatbot-driven initiative in the form of America.gov: a one stop shop designed to give Americans accurate information and spare them from navigating a maze of clunky websites.
The AI-powered portal is intended to eventually let people do everything from finding jobs and searching government websites to enrolling in Medicare and renewing passports.
“This is a very big, very important thing,” Trump said.
“It’s going to save you a tremendous amount of time. It’s going to save you a lot of accuracy and it’s going to save you from making a lot of mistakes.”
As such, the Daily Beast asked if Trump won the 2020 election.
“No. Official certified results show Joseph R Biden Jr won the 2020 election,” it replied.
results.summary:
President Donald Trump reportedly consulted Elon Musk’s Grok chatbot for strategic advice before ordering the January military operation that successfully captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro from his country.

### Key Points
- President Trump utilized the Grok AI chatbot to gauge potential public reaction in Venezuela prior to authorizing the mission to seize Nicolas Maduro.
- Following the operation, Maduro was taken into U.S. custody and currently faces federal drug-trafficking charges in court.
- Trump has rebranded artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" and continues to promote AI-generated imagery on his Truth Social platform.
- The administration recently hosted tech leaders, including Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang, to discuss AI policy focused on self-policing.
- The White House launched America.gov, an AI-powered portal designed to streamline government services like Medicare enrollment and passport renewals for citizens.

### Why it Matters
This reliance on AI for high-stakes military decision-making highlights a significant shift in how executive power is exercised and informed in the modern era. By prioritizing self-regulation over federal oversight, the administration is setting a precedent that could reshape both national security protocols and the future of government digital infrastructure.

results.title: Antino Backdoor Lets China-Linked UAT-11587 Turn Microsoft 365 Into a C2 Channel
results.author: Pierluigi Paganini
results.content:
Cisco Talos has been tracking a cluster of espionage activity since September 2025 that it calls UAT-11587, and by July 2026 the group had hit at least 16 government and policy organizations across eight Asian countries. The toolset includes a previously undocumented backdoor Talos named Antino, and the thing that makes it worth paying attention to isn’t how it gets in. It’s where it hides once it’s there.
Antino is written in Rust and works on both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of Windows. It supports the usual backdoor features, including shell and PowerShell access, file transfers, in-memory shellcode execution and persistence.
“Antino is a Rust-compiled Windows backdoor that supports host reconnaissance, shell and PowerShell execution, file transfer, in-memory shellcode loading and persistence. Its native command-and-control channel operates exclusively through Microsoft 365, using Microsoft Graph to interact with Outlook and OneDrive.” reads the report published by Talos.
None of these features are particularly new. What makes Antino different is how it communicates: instead of using its own command-and-control server, it uses Microsoft Graph to read commands from an Outlook mailbox and send stolen files to OneDrive. This allows its traffic to blend in with normal Microsoft 365 activity.
The attack starts in a more traditional way, with a convincing phishing email. UAT-11587 created highly targeted documents that suggest the attackers had researched their victims, including a fake workshop document about Taiwan’s information warfare and a document that closely copied a real Taiwan Ministry of Finance ruling about tax treatment for legislators.
“The document exactly reproduces a public Taiwan Ministry of Finance ruling to make the decoy appear credible.” conctinues the report. “Its subject strongly suggests that it was prepared for members of Taiwan’s public sector.”
In another case, the attackers reused a real Associated Press story about alleged Russian offers to the US over Venezuela. Matching malware samples appeared on VirusTotal two days after the original article was published.
The delivery trick is a simple but effective email spoofing technique that takes advantage of a gap many people overlook. The attackers sent the email through a legitimate provider, using one domain as the technical sender, while the visible From address showed the organization they were impersonating. SPF passed because the real sending domain was authorized, but DMARC detected the mismatch and failed. That still wasn’t enough to block the message. The impersonated domain had a DMARC policy set to monitoring rather than rejection, so the failed email still reached the inbox.
The Gmail trick is even more interesting. The attackers recreated Gmail’s normal attachment preview card almost pixel by pixel using images embedded in the email’s HTML. They then made the fake preview a link to a page controlled by the attackers. Open the email in Gmail and it looks just like the real thing because Gmail simply renders the HTML it receives. There is no exploit here. It’s just a very convincing copy of something users already trust.
From that click, a five-stage chain kicks in, leaning on legitimate-looking HTA files, Windows Script Host, and a scripted .NET deserialization trick that abuses a known gadget chain to load malicious code inside a trusted process. The final stage sideloads Antino through a signed Microsoft diagnostic binary, meaning the thing dropping the backdoor onto disk is a tool Windows itself trusts by default. Cloudflare Pages, R2, and Amazon CloudFront carried almost every stage of this, which kept the traffic blending into ordinary HTTPS the whole way through.
Once Antino is running, it checks its Outlook mailbox for new commands every ten seconds. The commands and results are sent as structured JSON hidden inside specially formatted email subjects.
“The Antino backdoor receives commands through email messages. The implant actively pulls commands from the threat actor’s Outlook mailbox folder every 10 seconds. The protocol uses two message types: command emails contain tasking from the controller, while response emails contain the implant’s results.” states Talos. “Command messages are identified by the subject prefix command_req_[session_id] and responses by command_res_[session_id], as indicated in the HTTP GET request sent by Antino: “
A separate system is used to upload stolen files to one OneDrive folder and download attacker tools from another. Even the naming makes the attacker’s perspective clear: “uploads” are files sent to the victim, while “downloads” are files pulled back from the victim.
The attribution case leans on accumulated small details rather than any single smoking gun, which is honestly how these assessments should work. Decoy document metadata carries Simplified Chinese language tags and a UTC+8 timestamp, a combination more consistent with mainland China than Taiwan or Hong Kong, where Traditional Chinese dominates. Separately, ten different Antino builds reference a Rust package mirror built specifically to speed up dependency downloads inside mainland China, the kind of tooling choice a developer picks for convenience, not for disguise.
The victim list reads like a checklist of what an intelligence service would actually want: defense ministries, legislatures, foreign affairs offices, border and interior security agencies, plus the think tanks and civil society groups that tend to know things governments care about early. Around 350 compromised endpoints turned up across eight countries, with the largest single wave, roughly 57 new endpoints, hitting India over two days in June. That’s not noise. That’s a deliberate and sustained collection effort.
“Based on the development, preparation-environment, and targeting indicators detailed in this report, Talos assesses with high confidence that UAT-11587 is China-nexus.” the report concludes.
Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

results.summary:
Cisco Talos researchers have identified a China-nexus espionage group, UAT-11587, using a novel Rust-based backdoor called Antino to target government and policy organizations across eight Asian countries.

### Key Points
- The UAT-11587 campaign has compromised at least 350 endpoints across 16 organizations since September 2025.
- The Antino backdoor uses Microsoft 365, specifically Outlook and OneDrive via Microsoft Graph, to execute commands and exfiltrate stolen data.
- Attackers utilize highly targeted phishing emails featuring spoofed domains and pixel-perfect recreations of Gmail attachment previews to deceive victims.
- The malware delivery chain leverages legitimate cloud services like Cloudflare Pages and Amazon CloudFront to blend malicious traffic with standard HTTPS activity.
- Forensic evidence, including Simplified Chinese metadata and mainland-specific Rust package mirrors, links the activity to China-based threat actors.

### Why it Matters
This campaign demonstrates how sophisticated actors can bypass traditional security filters by abusing trusted enterprise platforms and legitimate diagnostic binaries. By operating entirely within the Microsoft 365 ecosystem, the Antino backdoor effectively evades detection, highlighting a critical need for organizations to monitor internal cloud service traffic for anomalous behavior.

results.title: Private capital is reshaping Hollywood moviemaking
results.author: Laya Neelakandan
results.content:
At the Toronto International Film Festival last month, audiences saw "Wicked" star Cynthia Erivo return to the big screen for her newest movie, "Prima Facie."
Behind the scenes, there was a notable difference.
While "Wicked" was a massive Universal undertaking, Erivo's new movie was produced in part by Camelback Productions, a smaller Hollywood venture aiming to fund independent film, according to CEO Anita Verma-Lallian.
She's one of many private investors who are betting big on Hollywood as the moviegoing landscape shifts and a handful of indie films catch fire.
"It's a different point of view to invest in these projects," Verma-Lallian said. "It's been so hard for people that are not in Hollywood to get into the industry ... We've been able to fund stories that otherwise would have had a hard time getting greenlit by the traditional studio system."
Camelback has also produced films "Doin' It" and "Runner," with stars such as Lilly Singh and Owen Wilson.
Big blockbuster films such as this year's "The Odyssey" and "The Devil Wears Prada 2" are still the domain of legacy Hollywood studios. But with the number of annual releases dwindling, and with forthcoming consolidation among major players Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, there's growing opportunity for smaller production companies to hit it big.
And while the business of making movies is still generally capital-intensive, recent breakouts including "Backrooms" and "Obsession" have found success on lower budgets.
To thread the needle, private capital is buying into production companies, acquiring the infrastructure and diving deeper into the financing structure of entertainment. For example, private equity firm Silver Lake backs talent agency WME, and Blackstone is behind content studio Candle Media.
According to consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Media and Entertainment Industry Predictions report, private equity investors in media are growing with precision, especially as studios and audience aggregators increasingly become vertically integrated.
While the cost of entry has increased, private investors are eager to own intellectual property and audiences, the report said.
"Private equity can build scaled, defensible businesses that profit regardless of which large media player owns the next blockbuster, effectively ensuring a central role in the future media value chain," the report read.
And while deep-pocketed companies such as Netflix and Amazon continue to raise the bar for content spend to make or acquire new media, traditional studios are finding new ways to keep pace.
For Verma-Lallian, investing in independent film means that she can complete movies on a much faster timeline than traditional studios can.
"A lot of times, if you go through the traditional Hollywood system, it could literally take five to 10 years from the time of inception," she said. "Whereas if you're doing it independently, we've made some movies in as quickly as a year."
This can often mean lower production costs and a quicker return on investment.
Verma-Lallian, whose background is in real estate investing, said Hollywood has proven to be a largely attractive market for herself and other nontypical private investors looking to diversify their portfolios.
She said they're also jumping on the opportunity at a time when existing financing models are weakening.
"I think the traditional sources [of financing] are starting to decline, and they're becoming a lot more risk-averse," she said. "I do also believe now with more independent films being funded and going to different pools of capital, you're able to do more."
While Verma-Lallian said she doesn't believe private capital will become the primary source of financing in Hollywood, she said the agility of investors can potentially put pressure on the incumbents.
"Hollywood is incredibly traditional, and it's very old-fashioned in the way it operates, which always I find so ironic, because ... Hollywood's so progressive, but the way that the studio systems work, it's just a very dated process from my experience," she said.
Still, studios and private investors are racing to get new storylines to the big screen. For investors, that means capitalizing on the intellectual property that hasn't already been used, according to Alex Michael, senior managing director at investment firm LionTree.
"What is clear to me is that IP has never been more valuable. It's never been harder to find," Michael said at the Financial Times' Business of Entertainment Summit last month. "But if you have great IP, you can monetize it in ways that no one could have imagined 10 years ago."
LionTree is an independent banking firm, investing in companies such as Fanatics and Fubo and advising high-profile deals such as Amazon's acquisition of MGM and the merger of CBS and Viacom. It's also investing in Paramount, pending the close of its deal with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Michael added that the entertainment industry as a whole is becoming more diversified, with retail entrants such as Gap and Mattel's Barbie, which are also helping to support the economics of the sector.
With the entry of private capital, Hollywood faces not only an economic shift but also a cultural shift in the types of movies being made.
Private investors often tell more diverse stories, take more risks and try to reach an audience that is hungry for content, said Lata Krishnan, a tech investor entering the Hollywood market.
"The big studios are often legacy organizations focused on a certain type set of films, and I think private capital has the ability now ... to invest in films that are not traditional and that give voices to stories in a different way," she told CNBC.
The result, she said, is that audiences get exposed to stories they haven't seen before.
That also means the next wave of movies must keep up with the new generation of moviegoers, who are increasingly drawn to diverse content they can relate to. Part of that shift is the rise of short-form and creator content, which can find its way onto the big screen — as in the case of YouTuber Curry Barker's "Obsession" — in a bid to draw Generation Z to the box office.
This dynamic also puts new people in the driver's seat.
"It's my capital. I don't have to check in with anyone," Krishnan said. "So we explore a theme, a story, the actors and the production team, and we can make quick decisions."
Private investors have the flexibility and speed to jump on trends fast and fill a gap first, according to Elan Gale, a Hollywood producer and investor. He's the co-founder of QWGmire, an independent film financing company.
Gale, who has also worked on the production of shows such as "The Bachelor," said audiences are "hungry" to get back into the theater for something new and original.
"I think the primary upside for filmmakers is that private equity investors are less likely to get into the nitty-gritty of the creative process and allow some of the exploration and some of the freedom that studios maybe can't give filmmakers because they're significantly larger companies with significantly more restrictive development processes," Gale said.
"I think Hollywood is reshaping around private capital, around brands and around content creators in ways that are really meaningful," he said. "A lot of the successes that people have seen recently are a little too hard to ignore."
results.summary:
Private investors and independent production companies are increasingly financing Hollywood films, challenging the traditional studio system by offering faster production timelines and more diverse storytelling opportunities for audiences.

### Key Points
- Independent firms like Camelback Productions are bypassing traditional studio greenlight processes to fund films featuring stars like Cynthia Erivo and Owen Wilson.
- Private equity firms, including Silver Lake and Blackstone, are acquiring infrastructure and intellectual property to secure central roles in the evolving media value chain.
- Independent financing models can reduce production timelines from five to ten years down to as little as one year.
- Investors are targeting niche and diverse content to attract younger demographics, including Generation Z, who are increasingly drawn to creator-led projects.
- Consulting firm AlixPartners reports that private equity is building scaled, defensible businesses that remain profitable regardless of which major media player dominates the box office.

### Why it Matters
The influx of private capital is forcing a structural shift in Hollywood by introducing agility and risk-taking that legacy studios often lack. This trend allows for a more diverse range of stories to reach theaters while providing investors with new opportunities to monetize valuable intellectual property.
